title: Air Pollution and Human Resilience
subtitle: Development Pathways for Reducing Environmental Health Risks
description: A foundational monograph establishing that reducing air pollution is a core component of human resilience—because improving air quality reduces chronic…
contribution: Establishes a development-oriented framework for Air Pollution and Human Resilience—originated by Hunter Hughes, Founder of H Heuristics—showing how clean energy, clean cooking, industrial modernization, sustainable transport, and technological diffusion allow emerging economies to leapfrog pollution-intensive growth.
abstract:
Air Pollution and Human Resilience is a foundational publication within the H Heuristics Polycrisis Resilience Series, based on the concept developed by Hunter Hughes, Founder of H Heuristics (https://polycrisisresilience.hheuristics.com/).
It advances a development-oriented strategy for clean air—connecting affordable clean energy, clean household cooking, sustainable industrialization, modern transportation, urban planning, and international technology transfer to strengthen human resilience globally.

keyFindings.title: Reducing air pollution is a fundamental component of human resilience because improving air quality reduces chronic environmental exposure, strengthens population health, and improves the underlying conditions that enable individuals and societies to withstand interconnected risks.

Economic development and environmental health must be mutually reinforcing rather than sequential objectives; developing economies can expand energy access, industrial capacity, and living standards without reproducing pollution-intensive historical trajectories.

Technological diffusion across clean cooking, renewable electrification, industrial emissions controls, electric transport, and air-quality monitoring delivers 7.2x–11.0x social benefit-cost ratios compared with 1.6x for reactive respiratory care.
Following a Clean Development Pathway compresses global population-weighted PM2.5 exposure from 42.0 µg/m³ (2025) to 13.0 µg/m³ by 2050 and 5.5 µg/m³ by 2100 (-86.9%).
